comment: Tables exempt from the FORCE-RLS + per-operation policy manifest gate (tools/check-rls-manifest.mjs). Every entry must be {"table": string, "reason": string} and be approved by {{SECURITY_OWNERS}} — an exemption without a reviewed reason is a gate bypass. The only entries are the audit trail's, and they are exempt from THAT GATE'S MODEL, not from scrutiny: an append-only table must have no UPDATE or DELETE policy, which is the opposite of what a per-operation manifest requires. tools/check-tenancy.mjs judges them instead, by rules that are strictly stronger. Note that schema-rls still checks one thing about them unconditionally, because its non-public-schema rule does not consult this list: that `audit` is absent from [api].schemas. One more key, `mfaRailUnused`, is not a table exemption: it records the reviewed decision that no table here warrants a second factor yet, the only way the MFA helpers may be defined with no policy using them, and the gate reds it as stale the day a policy does (2.0.0).

mfaRailUnused.reason: The default scaffold has no table that warrants a second factor yet: the spine defines private.mfa_satisfied() and private.mfa_is_required() in every install so the rail is ready, and the worked example's notes table, the one table that carried it, ships only with `init --with-demo`. Which data warrants aal2 is a product decision, not a scaffold default. The first table that does takes the RESTRICTIVE policy docs/adr/20260812-mfa-aal2.md describes, and this row goes with it (schema-rls reds it as stale the moment a policy uses the rail).

exempt.reason: Append-only by design, so the four-per-operation policy model this gate enforces is the wrong shape: it has an INSERT policy (for app_audit_writer, asserting the row's actor matches the database's own opinion of who is acting), a SELECT policy (rank >= 30, for app_audit_reader), and DELIBERATELY NO UPDATE OR DELETE POLICY — that absence is layer 1 of four. It is also unreachable by the supabase-js client suite by construction (schema `audit` is absent from [api].schemas, so PostgREST will not serve it), which is why it cannot be an ISOLATION_TARGETS row. Enforcement lives in tools/check-tenancy.mjs (the four immutability layers, the writer/reader split, the audit trigger on every org-scoped table) and in the pgTAP suite, which asserts UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE all raise 42501 against a live database. See docs/adr/20260202-audit-trail.md.

The DEFAULT partition of audit.events, and a partition is never independently policied: RLS is enabled and FORCEd on it with ZERO policies on purpose, which makes direct access deny-all while writes routed through the parent are judged by the parent's policies (verified against PostgreSQL 17). Requiring per-operation policies here would mean adding policies whose only effect is to WEAKEN it. The monthly partitions are created at runtime by audit.ensure_partitions() and never appear in migration text at all; this one is exempted explicitly because it is the single partition a migration creates.

Global reference data with no tenant dimension, so the isolation matrix has nothing to prove about it: an ISOLATION_TARGETS row needs an owner column, and there is none — every signed-in caller sees the same published ceilings. It IS fully policied (ENABLE + FORCE, SELECT true to authenticated, deny-all INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) and clients hold only SELECT; changing a default is a migration. The exemption is from the per-tenant isolation registries, not from RLS.

Holds only NEGOTIATED OVERRIDES, so it is empty in every fresh database and in every CI run — which means the isolation matrix has no row to prove anything with, and its positive control ('A must see its own row') could never pass. It is fully policied (ENABLE + FORCE, member-scoped SELECT, deny-all INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to authenticated) and clients hold SELECT only; the counter it caps, public.org_usage, shares the identical scope predicate, and the pgTAP structural suite (rls_targets) asserts both tables' shape.

The per-org usage COUNTER, written only by the quota triggers of a metered table (through app_quota_writer). A scaffold with no metered table has none, so it is empty in every fresh database and in every CI run — the isolation matrix has no row to prove anything with, and its positive control ('A must see its own row') could never pass. It is fully policied (ENABLE + FORCE, member-scoped SELECT, deny-all INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to authenticated), clients hold SELECT only, and the pgTAP structural suite keeps it in rls_targets. The first table a project meters gives it rows: add it to ISOLATION_TARGETS in tests/rls/db-context.ts then and delete this row (the notes vertical `init --with-demo` plants is the worked example).

Append-only by design like audit.events two entries up, and one notch stricter: it has an INSERT policy (for app_auth_trail_writer, the hook functions' owner), DELIBERATELY NO UPDATE OR DELETE POLICY (layer 1 of the same four), and — unlike the audit trail — NO SELECT POLICY FOR ANY ROLE: the read posture is the operator's own database access, recorded in migration 20260816000000_auth_event_trail.sql, and the pgTAP suite asserts the ABSENCE of a read policy structurally so one appearing is a finding. Unreachable by the client suite by construction (schema auth_trail is absent from [api].schemas), so it cannot be an ISOLATION_TARGETS row. Enforcement lives in the migration's four layers and supabase/tests/auth_trail.test.sql, which proves immutability against the superuser and client denial at the schema wall against a live database. See docs/adr/20260816-auth-event-trail.md.

The DEFAULT partition of auth_trail.events — same reasoning as audit.events_default one entry up: a partition is never its own surface, and this one exists so a write can land when partition maintenance has stopped. It carries its own ENABLE + FORCE (RLS is not inherited), zero policies (deny-all for direct access), and its own BEFORE TRUNCATE twin, all asserted by the pgTAP suite.
